title: The oldest poems
hook: among the oldest Buddhist verses, first put into English in full in 1881

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Long Discourses, and your line was the long way home. Did a big question find its way to a real person? Today, a new collection, and a much older sound. Day five hundred seventy-six.

In 1881, in Oxford, a volume came off the press: the tenth book in a series called the Sacred Books of the East. Inside were two Buddhist texts in English, side by side. One was the Dhammapada, translated by Max Muller. The other was a collection of poems, translated from the Pali by a Danish scholar named Viggo Fausboll. Some readers think a few of those poems belong to the oldest layers of the Buddhist canon. Today we open that second book. Today's word: Sutta Nipata.
screen: `OXFORD, 1881.` → `A DANISH SCHOLAR'S TRANSLATION.` → `A SECOND BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata means something like the collection of discourses, or the gathering of suttas. It's a small book of short pieces, most of them in verse, sorted into five chapters. Some you may have met: the discourse on loving-kindness, the discourse on blessings, the rhinoceros poem. Others are less familiar. Why do some scholars call parts of it old? They give a few reasons. The language of some verses is archaic, closer to older Indian poetry. The fourth and fifth chapters, called the Chapter of Eights and the Way to the Beyond, are explained line by line by another text inside the canon itself, the Niddesa. To these scholars, a commentary inside the canon suggests the poems were already old and already puzzling while the canon was still being shaped. And the picture of life in them is spare: wanderers, forests, rivers, almost no buildings, very little organization. Some scholars read that as a window onto the earliest days. Others are more cautious and say old verses and newer ones sit side by side. That's why we're reading it slowly. These are poems meant to be said aloud and remembered. You'll hear refrains, lines that come back verse after verse, the way a song comes back to its chorus. Over the next weeks: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros, a plowman, a spirit with a threat, and a long list of blessings.
screen: `THE COLLECTION OF DISCOURSES` · `FIVE CHAPTERS, MOSTLY VERSE` · `A COMMENTARY INSIDE THE CANON` · `POEMS MEANT TO BE SAID ALOUD` · then, large: `OLD WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse aloud. Here's one from the other book in that 1881 volume, Max Muller's Dhammapada, a line that calls itself old. Say it with me, slowly, in a normal speaking voice: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule. Now say it once more on your own, a little slower. Notice the sound in your mouth and the quiet after it. Then sit with the breath and let the line settle. The bell holds the time.
screen: `FOR HATRED DOES NOT CEASE BY HATRED AT ANY TIME.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata. The collection of discourses: a small book of short pieces, mostly verse, some of them very old. Today's word.
Your line: old words. Sometime today, say that verse aloud once more, to yourself or to someone else, and let an old sentence be heard again. Day five hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 576 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SNAKE SHEDS ITS SKIN.`

howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, especially the discourses on loving-kindness, blessings and the jewel, are among the texts chanted in Theravada temples and homes, and the collection is studied in monasteries.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old Buddhist text is old because the Buddha lived long ago.
what it means: within the canon some layers are older than others, and parts of the Sutta Nipata look like some of the earliest.
what a scholar hears: archaic meter and language, a canonical commentary (the Niddesa) on its last chapters, and spare forest settings point some scholars to an early date.

notes: Hook says 1881 was the first full English translation: Mutu Coomaraswamy published a partial English Sutta Nipata in 1874, so the voice line about English readers should not be read as a first-ever claim.

Check the exact wording and punctuation of Max Müller's Dhammapada 5 (SBE 10, 1881): 'For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.' The script reads the dash as a semicolon in speech.
Fausbøll's Sutta Nipata is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing from it is quoted; all Sutta Nipata material in this block is paraphrased.
Confirm the count of about seventy suttas (commonly 71 or 72 depending on division) and the chapter names Atthakavagga and Parayanavagga.
The dating claims are presented as a common scholarly view with caution noted.
